title: Two Truths and a Lie
logline: Orientation week: a poet appoints himself Cal's keeper, an anonymous account starts posting the third floor's secrets, and the oldest house on Elm Row sends its pledge master to collect a promise.
previously: RICHARD (text): "It was funny. Next time make it funny at someone else's expense."
CAL (on the keg table): "To my father, who couldn't be here today. Which is the most Whitaker sentence ever spoken."
MARGAUX: "Nobody knows. Not your friends, not whoever's been blowing up your phone. Nobody." CAL: "Okay."
DEV: "For what it's worth? I'd have driven you."
Nora pins an old Polaroid beside an empty oval and writes: WHO WAS ON THE DOCK?
calNow: Cal is still charming his way through every room, but tonight he chose the truth with Dev and the performance with everyone else. He has traded a private secret with Margaux, a promise with his father and a lie or two with the new friends who are starting to matter, and he is not sure which of them he can afford to lose.

cast.name: Dev Okafor
cast.impression: The nicest guy on campus. He carried your heaviest box, built a crooked loft bed with you, and sat on the hallway floor when you needed someone there. You told him the truth about your father and he said he'd have driven you. He's carrying something he hasn't told you.

cast.name: Priya Raman
cast.impression: A hurricane in a slip dress with a prop skull, who decided you were her best friend in about nine seconds. You hid her from her mother and let her read one line of your notebook. She asked if it was real, and you said it was fiction. You asked if she was okay, then never saw her answer.

cast.name: Nora Castellanos
cast.impression: A Herald reporter who is faster than you and wrote you off as a rich idiot. She turned down your coffee and then quoted your toast word for word. She has her own reasons for being at Whitlock.

cast.name: Margaux Vance
cast.impression: Perfect from every angle, and she knows your father. You kissed her on a roof and went home with her. Her one rule: nobody knows. She asks careful questions, and her phone is the one thing that frightens her.

cast.name: Danny Doyle
cast.role: High-school junior · Busboy at Dot's Diner
cast.impression: A seventeen-year-old busboy with a pencil behind his ear and a side hustle. You bought what he was selling. He told you not to get caught, because his sister would kill him.

cast.name: Richard Whitaker
cast.impression: Sent a car instead of coming. After midnight he texted in his own words, liked the toast, and got your promise to rush. The first 'Proud of you' in years, with a price tag on it.

blocks.text: INT. WHITAKER COMMONS, DINING HALL. MORNING (TUE 08-25, 8:40 A.M.)

Four hours of sleep. Cal Whitaker walks into breakfast with his hair still wet and the specific glow of a boy who has not yet thought about anything that happened last night, because thinking would ruin it.

The dining hall is a cathedral somebody filled with waffle irons. Vaulted ceiling, oak beams, two hundred freshmen eating cereal under stained glass. Over the omelet station hangs an oil portrait of CHARLES WHITAKER, Class of 1961, in a gray suit, one hand on a globe, looking down at the egg line like he's about to foreclose on it. Cal's grandfather. Cal avoids his eyes. He always has.

He grabbed the only clean thing within reach on his way out the door. He realizes what it was only when the card swiper, LORRAINE, sixties, a townie with reading glasses on a beaded chain, swipes his ID, looks at his chest, and raises both eyebrows above the frames.

blocks.name: LORRAINE
blocks.text: Pledging Kappa, hon? Bold.

He looks down. KAPPA LAMBDA, across his chest, in white Greek letters, three inches tall. Her sweatshirt. The sleeves stop two inches short of his wrists. It smells like her perfume, and under the perfume, like her.

He grabbed the only clean thing within reach: a navy Rho quarter-zip somebody threw at him on the Kappa lawn last night. Lorraine, the card swiper, sixties, beaded glasses chain, looks at the crest on his chest and sighs like a woman who has seen forty years of boys in that exact zipper. Pledging the Rho already, hon? Of course you are.

At the long table by the windows sits the Kappa Lambda freshman-orientation brunch, twelve sisters in matching white Supergas, and at the head of it, MARGAUX VANCE, pressed, glossy, pearl studs, reading a printed copy of the Wall Street Journal like it's 1987 and she's a man. As if last night happened to a different woman. As if it happened to nobody.
Six Kappas see the sweatshirt at the same time. It's like watching a flock of birds turn. One of them actually puts down her spoon.
Margaux does not look up. She turns a page. Her phone, face-down beside her black coffee, buzzes once. Then Cal's buzzes in his pocket, in reply, like the two phones are talking about him.

msgs.text: Both.

blocks.text: It takes him a second. His last text to her, at 2 a.m.: Is that a request or a warning? Both. Then the dots, and then:

msgs.text: Take it off or own it. Those are the options.

blocks.name: > margaux
blocks.text: You flirt like you're being graded. Get dressed like it too.

Lorraine hands back his ID. The omelet guy is waiting with a ladle. His grandfather is watching from the wall. Two hundred people, one wrong sweatshirt, and a girl who said nobody knows, eating a grapefruit thirty feet away without a flicker.

choices.label: Own it: walk past the Kappa table and wave

reaction.text: He picks up his tray like a man accepting an award and walks the long way around, right past the Kappa table, and gives the whole row a slow, gracious wave, a candidate on a rope line.

reaction.name: KAPPA JUNIOR
reaction.text: WHO GAVE YOU THAT?
The bookstore sells them to boys who want to be near us. It's a whole economy. We get a percentage.
The table explodes. Cal laughs too, bows, and keeps walking. The laugh is at him, and he takes it like a tip. Under the table, without moving her shoulders, Margaux types.

msgs.text: Bold. Stupid. Noted.

choices.label: Turn it inside out right there in the omelet line

reaction.text: He sets the tray on the sneeze guard, peels the sweatshirt off over his head in front of the eggs, turns it inside out with two snaps like a man folding a flag, and pulls it back on. Plain gray fleece, seams showing, a tag at the back of his neck like a price.

Lorraine applauds, three slow claps. The omelet guy says, "Respect." Across the room, Margaux Vance, for one half-second, almost laughs. He sees it start at the corner of her mouth. She covers it with her coffee cup and holds the cup there far longer than coffee requires.

msgs.text: That was almost charming.
Almost.

choices.label: Text her back: “Come take it off me yourself.”

reaction.text: He takes the table in full view of hers, sets down his tray, and types it with his thumb while buttering toast with the other hand.

msgs.text: Come take it off me yourself.

reaction.text: Across the room, he watches her read it. Nothing on her face. Not a muscle. She sips her coffee. A Kappa next to her asks her something about a mixer and she answers in complete sentences. Then:

msgs.text: Not in daylight, Whitaker.

reaction.text: He's halfway through a triumphant bite when the second one comes.

msgs.text: Maybe not in daylight.

reaction.text: He reads it six times. The toast goes cold. Maybe. The most expensive word he's ever been sent.

blocks.text: Act One · Two Truths
INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD-FLOOR COMMON ROOM. DAY (TUE 2:00 P.M.)

Mandatory floor icebreaker. Two couches that have absorbed sixty years of secrets, a dead ficus, a dozen freshmen on folding chairs. JUNE, the RA, holds a laminated agenda and the face of a woman on her last nerve.

blocks.name: JUNE
blocks.text: Our Orientation Leader is running a little late. He's a sophomore. He's very... he'll explain himself.

Priya is cross-legged on the arm of a couch with Kevin the skull in her lap. Dev sits beside Cal, hands on knees, the posture of a man who has never been late to anything. A lacrosse boy named Hunter is doing calf raises for no reason.
Eleven minutes late: a camel overcoat in August, a silk scarf, a steel thermos of something extremely not coffee. Pale, sharp, starved-Victorian beautiful. This is SIMON ACHTERBERG, 19.
I'm Simon. I'm your Orientation Leader, which means the university has trusted me with your souls for seventy-two hours, which is a clerical error. Sit down, Hunter. Nobody needs calves.
He takes over the room in ninety seconds, diagnosing everyone in the circle with a Victorian ailment.
Hysteria. Obviously. The fun kind.
Thank you.
A nobly concealed consumption. You'll cough into a handkerchief and refuse to burden anyone. (to Hunter) Gout.

blocks.name: HUNTER
blocks.text: I'm eighteen.
And yet.
Then he gets to Cal, and stops, and smiles, slow. "Oh. You're the boy who introduced himself to the Herald as a building." The room laughs. Somebody whispers "like the building" in a voice.
Then he gets to Cal, and stops, and smiles, slow. "Oh. You're the boy whose grandfather is a building." The room laughs.
Then he gets to Cal, and stops, and smiles, slow. "Oh. You're the boy whose grandfather is a building." The room laughs.

Three people in the circle raise invisible cups at him at once and say it together, like a chant at a game: "The most Whitaker sentence ever spoken." The toast video is in every freshman group chat. Someone has already made it a sound.
Simon studies Cal's face a beat too long, like a man looking for a word in a language he used to speak.
Inherited melancholy. With complications.
He hid me in a closet yesterday and seduced my mother. In that order.
June writes this down. Nobody knows why. June doesn't know why.
Wonderful. Now. Two Truths and a Lie. Three statements, one of them false, and I'll tell you which, because I am never wrong. I don't do this with my mind. I do it with your hands.

He goes four for four. Hunter: lie, "and it's the one about your mother, Hunter, don't ever do that again." Dev's three are so wholesome the room boos; Simon calls the lie instantly, and Dev's delighted confession is a second lie, which only Cal notices.
Mr. Whitaker. Entertain us.
Every face turns. Cal knows this game. He's played it at Choate mixers and his father's Christmas parties. The trick is picking which true things to spend.

choices.label: “I've read one book four times. I swam competitively. I've never been in love.”

reaction.text: The soft set. The room debates. The consensus is the swimming: he doesn't look like a swimmer, says the Shaker Heights girl, he looks like a man who owns a boat.
The love one. Obviously.
Why obviously?
Because you said it like a door closing.

The room oohs. Cal grins and shrugs and lets it be a joke. Under the noise, Priya, very quietly, from the arm of the couch: "What book?" He pretends not to hear. Next to him, Dev nods once at "swam competitively," like a man filing a receipt.

choices.label: “My name's on a building. I'm pledging the Rho. My father's coming to Convocation.”

reaction.text: The swagger set. Groans at the building. A boo for the Rho. Simon doesn't even pause.
Your father's not coming.

Silence, a very short one. Then the room laughs, because it thinks it's a joke, a mean, perfect joke, and Simon lets it be one, bowing slightly. Cal laughs too, half a second late, a half-second that feels like falling down a step in the dark.
Dev doesn't laugh. Dev looks at his own hands.

choices.label: “I'm a Libra. I hate parties. I'm a terrible liar.”

reaction.text: The meta set. A big laugh. Simon is genuinely delighted; he puts down his thermos to clap.
They're all lies. You're a Pisces. You love parties. And you're the best liar in this room, which is saying something, because she's here.

He points at Priya. Priya stands on the couch and takes a deep, theatrical bow, Kevin held aloft. Everyone laughs. Cal laughs. Simon was right about the Pisces, which nobody told him, and Cal is still thinking about that when he notices that Priya, coming up from the bow, is the one person in the room who didn't laugh at all.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, STAIRWELL. CONTINUOUS (2:40 P.M.)
The icebreaker breaks. Simon catches Cal on the second-floor landing, under a window of wavy colonial glass, and leans on the banister like a man about to sell him a car.
You touch your left eyebrow when you lie.
I don't.
Thumb. Left side. Like a man checking his hairline is still there. You did it on the Libra. You did it just now, on "I don't." I'll keep it between us for a fee.
What's the fee?
The fee is I adopt you. You'll be my ward. I'll teach you which forks matter and which people do. In exchange, you let me watch.

He doesn't wait for an answer. He gives Cal the campus in four minutes flat, walking down the stairs backward like a tour guide, which he also is. Who matters. Who's pretending. Which dean drinks. Which a cappella group is a cult, and which is, legally, a church. The Herald: "small, angry, correct." The Rho: "old money, new lawyers." Kappa Lambda: "The pearls are real. The smiles are rented."
And then there's Margaux Vance. Kappa, Greenwich, perfect, terrifying. She'll be a senator's wife or a senator. Although.
Although?
The Vances sold the Nantucket house in June. Quietly. I read property transfers the way normal people read horoscopes. Nobody sells Nantucket, Calvin. You sell a kidney first. You sell a child.

Cal goes still. Not much. A boy pausing on a stair. But last night, on the Kappa lawn, with a drink in her hand, she asked him whether his father was still doing Nantucket for Labor Day. Like it was a calendar question. Like she was just making conversation about an island.

And he told her the truth about his father, that he didn't come, that Cal doesn't know his schedule, and she said Mine didn't either and then covered it like a spill. He doesn't say any of this to Simon. He doesn't say anything. He feels the place where the thumb wants to go.
Simon sees him go still. Simon sees everything. He files it with the expression of a man pocketing a coin off the sidewalk.
Interesting. Hold still.
He has his phone up before Cal can object. The click of a fake shutter.
For the ailments chart. I keep a chart. Give me your phone.
Cal, against every instinct he owns, gives it to him. Simon types for a long time, too long for a phone number, and hands it back. New contact: SIMON, YOUR GUARDIAN.

choices.label: “Fine. Adopt me. I'm house-trained, mostly.”

reaction.text: Simon claps, once, the way a judge bangs a gavel.
Wonderful. Your first lesson: never wear a sorority's sweatshirt to breakfast. I heard about it from three separate people before noon, and one of them was a dean.
Also, the wave. Brave. Insane. You waved at Kappa Lambda like a Kennedy at a funeral.
Also I heard you undressed at the eggs. Lorraine is telling people.
Also you smirked at your phone for nine minutes at breakfast. Whatever she said, it was in lowercase. I can always tell.
It becomes a bit immediately. By the bottom of the stairs Simon is calling him "my ward" to a passing junior, who says "Congratulations?" and keeps walking.

choices.label: Read him back: “You collect people so nobody collects you.”

reaction.text: You collect people so nobody collects you. If you're the one with the chart, nobody puts you on one.
It lands. Cal watches it land, the way he watches all of them land. For one second Simon's face is nineteen and alone, a boy in a coat that's too warm for August because the coat is the point.
Then it's gone.
Oh, you're horrible. I love you. We're going to be very bad for each other.
He takes out a cigarette and doesn't light it. He holds it between two fingers for the rest of the conversation, like a thing to do with his hands that isn't shaking.

choices.label: “Tell me more about the Vances.”

reaction.text: Simon's eyebrows rise slowly, like a theater curtain.
Oh no. Oh, you poor thing.
I'm asking for a friend.
You're asking with your whole face. I don't know anything. I suspect everything. That's my brand.

He gives it to him anyway: Margaux Vance and Brooks Hadley, the junior, the Rho pledge master. "The royal engagement. On, off, on, like a lighthouse." Cal has now heard the name Brooks Hadley three times in two days: from his father, from Margaux, and from a poet on a staircase. It's starting to sound like weather coming.

blocks.text: INT. SIMON'S ROOM, THORNE HOUSE. LATE AFTERNOON (TUE 5:15 P.M.)
A sophomore single wallpapered floor to ceiling with poems torn out of library books, pages overlapping like fish scales. A desk lamp with a green shade. Simon, alone, coat still on.
He sends the photo from the stairwell to a little printer on the windowsill. It whirs out: Cal on the landing, wavy light on his face, caught mid-stillness.

From under a library copy of Ariel he slides a manila folder, labeled in fountain pen: R.W. '06. He opens it. A color printout, slightly pixelated, from a holiday party: a ballroom, a banner reading WHITAKER LYLE · HAPPY HOLIDAYS 2006, and a younger RICHARD WHITAKER in black tie, mid-laugh, head thrown back, a glass in his hand.

Simon lays Cal's photo beside it. He looks from one to the other. Then he turns to the mirror on the back of his door and tilts his own jaw to the same angle as the two men on his desk, and holds it there, and looks for something.
He doesn't find it. Or he does. He closes the folder very gently, the way you close a door on someone sleeping.
INT. LOWELL HOUSE, DEV'S DOUBLE. EVENING (TUE 6:30 P.M.)

Dev is folding laundry with the precision of a man defusing it. Without looking up: "You good? After last night. The dad stuff." Cal says yes. Dev nods at a T-shirt. "Door's open." He means his literal door, propped with a sneaker. He also doesn't.

Then a knock on the frame, a knock so quiet it's almost an apology. A kid with one army-green duffel, a gray hoodie with the hood up indoors, and a laptop under his arm covered in the ghosts of peeled-off stickers, pale rectangles where something used to say something. This is YUSUF HADDAD, 18.
Haddad.
YUSUF. Oh my God. You exist. I told everyone you were cool. I had no evidence.
Yusuf looks around the double. He looks at the loft bed for a long, judicial time.
Who built this. It's not level.

Mr. Okafor's exact words, in Mr. Okafor's exact cadence, from a stranger from Dearborn who has never met Mr. Okafor. Dev and Cal look at each other and break at the same time, Dev folded over the laundry, Cal against the doorframe. Yusuf waits for them to finish, unbothered, like weather.
Who assembled this. It's not level.
Dev laughs so hard he has to sit on the laundry. Yusuf waits for him to finish, unbothered, like weather.
Who assembled this. It's not level.
Dev laughs so hard he has to sit on the laundry. Yusuf waits for him to finish, unbothered, like weather.
Cal's phone buzzes. An unknown number, 713.

msgs.text: Cal, this is Ngozi Okafor. Dev tells me I am your mother now.
Mothers require a photograph of the Tupperware. Clean. God bless.

blocks.text: I gave her your number. She made me. I'm so sorry. She's going to text you about the weather. She's going to send you Bible verses about the weather.

Cal saves it as MOM (OKAFOR). He doesn't tell anyone that. He photographs the Tupperware, which is not clean, which has jollof crust on it from last night, and he looks at it, and he decides to wash it first. That's a whole new feeling. He doesn't know where to put it.
Yusuf is unpacking the duffel in neat, square stacks: four hoodies, all gray. He speaks without turning around.
How'd you get a single as a freshman. Who'd you kill.

It's the second time someone's asked. June asked it yesterday as a joke. Yusuf isn't joking; Yusuf doesn't seem to have the gene. And Dev is right there, on the floor with the laundry, smiling at a sock. Dev, who heard the answer yesterday, on this floor, holding a drill. A lottery. Pure luck. Very lucky person.

choices.label: Repeat it: “Housing lottery. I'm very lucky.”

reaction.text: Housing lottery. I'm very lucky.
Dev smiles at the sock. "We're both lucky." It's warm. It's their handshake from yesterday. It's also the second time Cal has made him shake it.
There's no freshman single lottery. I read the housing PDF on the plane. Section four.
Silence. Long enough for Gerald, across the hall, to bang once.
It's a secret lottery. It's not in the PDF. Very exclusive. You have to know a guy.
Yusuf looks at Dev. Yusuf looks at Cal. Yusuf goes back to his hoodies. Cal owes Dev again, and they both know the rate is going up.

choices.label: Tell the truth: “My father made a call.”

reaction.text: My father made a call. In June. I didn't ask him to. I didn't ask him not to.
He says it to Yusuf. He says it at Dev. Dev stops folding. He nods, once, slowly, like a man receiving a library book back that was long overdue and is only a little damaged.
Yusuf says, "Okay," and that's the whole review. Later, when Yusuf goes to find the bathroom, Dev says, low:
The poker chip's still a poker chip, though.
I know.
Okay.
One lie down. One still standing, in Dev's pocket, warm from his hand.

choices.label: “I'm a Whitaker. It's on the building, man.”

reaction.text: I'm a Whitaker, man. It's on the building. You can see it from the window. I'll point it out.

Yusuf turns around and looks at him for three full seconds. He doesn't write anything down. He doesn't say anything. He just turns back to his hoodies. It is somehow the most devastating review Cal has ever received, and he has been reviewed by headmasters.

Dev laughs, to be kind, the way you'd catch a glass someone dropped. And the lottery is still sitting there in the middle of the room, between Cal and Dev, untouched, like a third bed nobody's sleeping in.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD-FLOOR HALLWAY. EVENING (TUE 6:40 P.M.)
Dev comes out of the double in khakis and brown church shoes, leather soles that click on the hallway boards. A white envelope sticks out of his back pocket. He has earbuds in.
Going for a run.
He stops in Cal's doorway on the way past. Deadpan, to the hinges: "Nice sweatshirt last night. I didn't see it. I'm a vault." He knocks twice on the frame, like closing the vault.

He doesn't wait for an answer. Cal, at the sink in his doorway with the Tupperware, watches him go down the stairs: the khakis, the shoes, the envelope. Nobody runs in church shoes. Behind him, in the double, Yusuf is watching Cal watch Dev. Neither of them says anything. They both go back inside.
INT. CAL'S SINGLE, LOWELL HOUSE. NIGHT (TUE 11:10 P.M.)

Priya knocks with her forehead. She has a yellow Post-it stuck to it that says GERALD in Sharpie, a two-liter bottle of Cheerwine and an unopened bag of Sour Patch Kids, which she holds like a clutch.
I've come as your radiator. It's a costume. It's for morale.

She does twenty minutes without stopping. Orientation is a hostage video with lanyards. June is "a beautiful soul trapped in a fire marshal." Simon: "I want to be him and I want to push him down the stairs, and I think that's what love is." Her mother has texted her eleven times today, mostly links about sunscreen. She's bright. She's fast. She's very, very funny, and the bag of Sour Patch Kids stays closed the whole time, its corners getting soft in her hand.
Then, sideways, while looking at Kevin on his shelf:
You said always, by the way. In writing. I have it in writing, Cal. "Always. Go to sleep, Raman." Screenshotted. Notarized.
I meant it.
You didn't come swimming, though.
I said u ok.
You said u ok with two question marks. Which is one question mark of love. I counted.

She tells it like a bit. She swam out to the buoy by herself, in her underwear, at eleven at night, and back. "And the lake is so cold it's like being forgiven." She laughs. It's a good laugh, a stage laugh, it hits the back row. He can't tell if it's real. He's been able to tell with everyone his whole life, and he can't tell with her.
She thanks him, sideways, for coming in after her last night. She says it to Kevin, not to him. She won't look at him. "You didn't have to." "I did." "You didn't," she says, and that's the end of it.
He offers her Mrs. Okafor's jollof. He's been rationing it like a war.
I ate. I ate so much. I ate a whole... I had a wrap. Huge wrap.
Then she sees it. Draped over the back of his desk chair. The sweatshirt. KAPPA LAMBDA, in white.
She picks it up by the shoulders, holds it out at arm's length like a dress in a shop. Then she brings it to her face and smells the collar. Her eyes go wide over the fleece.
Oh. Oh, this isn't from the bookstore. This is from a person. This smells like a person who owns a horse.

Margaux on the floor of her room in the dark, saying it to the wall: Nobody knows. Not your friends. Nobody. And Priya, who is his friend, who has the screenshot that says always, holding the sweatshirt up between them like evidence.

choices.label: “Long story. I promised I wouldn't tell it.”

reaction.text: Long story. I promised somebody I wouldn't tell it.
True, every word, and it keeps the promise. Priya gasps like he's slapped her in a period drama.
A secret. From me. From your emergency contact. I'm the one they call if you die, Cal.

She folds the sweatshirt with exaggerated, funereal care, sleeves crossed over the chest like a corpse, and lays it back on the chair. She's thrilled. She's also, under the thrill, a little wounded, and he can see the wound and the thrill trading places very fast.
I'll find out. I always find out.
She means it as a joke. It doesn't sound like one.

choices.label: “Bookstore. I'm a superfan. Very into sororities.”

reaction.text: Bookstore. I'm a superfan. Very into sororities. I have a poster of the Kappa Lambda founders over my bed. They're watching us right now.
She laughs, a real one this time, he thinks. She lets it go. She doesn't believe a word of it, and she lets him see that she doesn't, which is its own kind of gift, and also its own kind of receipt.
At the door, on her way out, she says, "Night, superfan," and touches the doorframe twice with two fingers. He'll learn later that she does that when she's filing something.

choices.label: Tell her: Margaux Vance, the roof, all of it

reaction.text: He tells her. The lawn, the roof, the champagne, the phone face-down on the slate. He leaves out the parts that are only his. He doesn't leave out much.
She sits down on his floor with her mouth open like a cartoon of a girl with her mouth open.
MARGAUX VANCE? Cal. CAL. Margaux Vance is not a person, she's a tax bracket.
Then, softer, picking at the corner of the Sour Patch Kids:
Is that why you didn't come?
Yeah.
Okay.
She says it the way people say okay when it isn't. Then she puts her hand flat on Kevin's skull and swears on him she'll never tell a soul. Kevin, as a witness, says nothing.
At the door she turns, hand on the frame. "Who called who, by the way? In your fiction." He doesn't answer. She doesn't push. She goes. Gerald bangs once behind her, like a door she didn't close.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD FLOOR. MORNING (WED 08-26, 7:04 A.M.)
Every phone on the third floor goes off at once.
Through the walls and two-hundred-year-old plaster: a dozen buzzes and chimes and one ringtone that is, inexplicably, a goat. It sounds like the building has been told something.

Cal surfaces from sleep with his face in the pillow and his phone vibrating against the floorboards like a trapped wasp. Instagram. A new account has tagged him. @lowell.three. Bio: third floor confidential. we live here too. Followers: 340. It has existed for nineteen minutes.

First post, 7:04 a.m. A vertical video. The Kappa lawn at sunset, string lights, two hundred people chanting WHI-TA-KER, COM-MONS, the camera low and to the left of the keg table, shaking with whoever's screaming the loudest.
It ends on him. On the table, cup raised, the field of phone lights: "Which is the most Whitaker sentence ever spoken." Freeze frame on his face. Caption: welcome to lowell 3. we have a legacy.
It ends on him, in the middle of the chant, the crowd shoving him toward the keg like a sacrifice. Freeze frame on his face. Caption: welcome to lowell 3. we have a legacy.
He swipes. Second slide. White text on black, in the typewriter font everyone uses for confessions.
overheard on the third floor: our legacy keeps a diary. sample: "the ice machine at the seaside motor inn sounded like someone choking, and i was the one who called." who'd you call, babe? 🧊📞

He reads it again. It doesn't change. The only sentence anyone has ever read, in lowercase, with emojis, on every phone on his floor. 212 likes by 7:20. A stranger: wait this is actually so sad?? Another: rich people trauma is so aesthetic. A third, just: 🧊.

He has done this before. Eleven years old, a motel room, a door with a chain, the carpet that smelled like chlorine and cigarettes. He's very good at sitting against doors. He doesn't write. He doesn't move. Gerald bangs once, like a neighbor through a wall.
Then a voice through the wood, close, like she's sitting against the other side of it.
Cal? Cal, I saw it. Open up. Please. I'm not leaving. I'll sleep here. I'll get a cot.

blocks.text: INT. PRIYA'S SINGLE, LOWELL HOUSE. MORNING (WED 7:15 A.M.)
He opens the door. She takes him by the wrist without a word and walks him two doors down to her room, the way you'd walk a drunk friend to a cab.
Priya opens her door before he can knock, like she's been waiting behind it.

Priya's room looks like a teenage girl's bedroom as designed by a set dresser who loves her: fairy lights, a wall of Polaroids already, three days in, a vintage Hamlet poster in Polish, Kevin's black beret hanging on the bedpost. The bed hasn't been slept in. The duvet has the shape of someone who sat on top of it all night.

She's devastated. She's furious on his behalf. She's pacing in the sleep mask and the Rutgers shirt, and it's a brilliant performance, and it's also completely real, and he can see both at once, which has never happened to him before. It's like seeing two colors in the same place.
I read it OUT LOUD, Cal. On Monday. With your door open. June was doing room checks. The whole hall could have heard me. Hunter was in the hall. Hunter was RIGHT THERE with a mini-fridge.
Priya.
This is my fault. This is literally my fault. I read your diary like it was a cereal box, out loud, in a hallway with acoustics.

Every word is true. She did read it aloud. The door was open. June was doing room checks. He was there. It's a story built entirely out of true things, which is the only kind he ever has trouble with.

She's already in the app. She's DMing @lowell.three, typing with both thumbs, fast and hard: TAKE IT DOWN COWARD. She shows him the screen like a receipt. Then a second one: i know where you live. we ALL know where you live. that's the PREMISE.
Your comment was perfect, by the way. "Buy the book." You're so good at that. It's scary. You just... do the thing, and everyone's on your side again.
And I would never, ever tell anyone about Margaux. Ever. You know that. I swore on Kevin. Kevin's binding.
Cal's phone lights up in his hand.
He saved it Monday afternoon off a business card, with Priya hiding in his closet behind his shoes: DR. LAKSHMI RAMAN. Her mother's card. In case Priya stops answering.

She cries into his shoulder, hard, like she's been holding it in a jar. And something in her body goes slack against him, a kind of relief, total and immediate, like a held breath let out. He'll think about that later, when he knows more. Right now it just feels like holding someone.

Promise.

He says it quietly. That's worse than shouting, and he knows it while he's doing it.
Her face does three things in one second: hurt, then fear, then fury, stacked like cards. The fear is the one he'll remember.
You think I'd... You actually think I'd...
She opens her door and points at the hallway with her whole arm, like an usher.
Get out. GET OUT. I'm the only person on this floor who's been NICE to you!

The door slams. He stands in the hall in his shirt with no shoes, with her mother's text in his pocket and no proof of anything. Through the door, after a second, he hears her crying, and then he hears her stop, very suddenly, like a tap turned off.

Your mom wants to know if you're eating.
The account is forgotten in a heartbeat. He watches it go. Priya goes white, all the way to the mouth, and then she laughs, too loud, a laugh with no floor under it.
She's insane. I eat. I eat constantly. I'm eating right now, spiritually. Give me that.
She takes his phone out of his hand and types back to her mother herself, fast: she's great!! eating like a horse lol -cal. She hits send and hands it back.

Her hands are shaking. Not much. Enough. He saw it. She saw him see it. For one second they just look at each other across the fairy lights, two people who are very good at being looked at, caught looking.

blocks.text: EXT. THE QUAD, OUTSIDE PRUITT HALL. MORNING (WED 8:55 A.M.)

The English writing placement exam is at nine in Pruitt Hall, the red-brick building with the Herald's basement windows at ankle height. Every freshman has to sit it. It decides which writing seminar you're put in, and, according to a rumor on the floor chat, which professor decides you're an idiot.
Cal hasn't slept enough. His sentence is on the internet. He has a pencil and a Commons coffee and the specific numbness of a person whose worst thing has been made public before breakfast.
Dev and Yusuf are walking the other way across the grass, toward the gate and Mill Street, Dev's arm around Yusuf's shoulders like they've known each other for years and not fifteen hours.
We're skipping the meal plan for Dot's. Yusuf has never had a real diner pancake. It's a human rights issue. Come.
I've had pancakes.
From a box. He's had pancakes from a BOX, Cal.
The doors of Pruitt Hall are open. A grad student with a clipboard is calling names from the steps.

choices.label: Take the exam and write the true thing

reaction.text: He goes up the steps. He doesn't know yet what he's going to write. That's a lie. He knows exactly.

reaction.text: He writes four flawless, funny pages about quitting the St. Anselm's swim team, almost none of it true: a coach with a toupee, a rival from Exeter, a dramatic exit in a Speedo during the national anthem. It's very good. It's the best armor he's ever built. He's out in forty minutes, and on the steps he realizes he can't remember a single sentence of it, which is how armor works.

reaction.text: He jogs to catch up. Dev cheers like he scored. Yusuf says nothing, but moves over on the sidewalk to make room for a third person, which, Cal will learn, is Yusuf for yes.

blocks.text: INT. PRUITT HALL, ROOM 104. DAY (WED 9:00 A.M.)

Forty freshmen in a sloped lecture room with radiators along the windows. Blue books. A proctor in a cardigan who looks like he's on the third year of a dissertation about one poem. On the board, in chalk, the prompt:
WRITE ABOUT A ROOM YOU LEFT. 40 MINUTES.
Around him, the sound of thirty-nine people beginning essays about their childhood bedrooms. Cal opens the blue book. He looks at the line for a long time. Then he writes the Seaside Motor Inn.
We see it in his hand. Small, fast, slanting left, the handwriting nobody's read.

"The best weekend of my life was the one where my mother didn't sleep. She picked me up from school on a Thursday with the windows down in March and said we were going to see the ocean in Maine because the ocean in Massachusetts was boring now. We ate lobster rolls at two in the morning in a parking lot. She bought me a kite shaped like a fish and flew it off the hood of the car. She sang every song on the radio, even the ads."

"The Seaside Motor Inn had an ice machine outside our door that sounded like someone choking. On the third night she was talking faster than the TV. She'd been talking since Thursday. She was explaining something to me about the way the lights on the water were a language, and she was so happy, and she was crying, and she wanted me to understand, and I did not understand. There was a phone on the nightstand with the motel's name on a strip of paper under the keypad. I took it into the bathroom and pulled the cord under the door."
"I was the one who called, and two weeks later she was gone, and I have been very careful about telephones ever since."
He doesn't write the ending. He doesn't know what the ending is. He looks at the page. His hand hurts. Nobody has ever read this, and in four minutes somebody is going to.

reaction.text: CALVIN WHITAKER, in block capitals, on the cover of the truest thing he's ever written.

It feels like stepping off the end of a dock at night: one second of nothing, then all of it at once. He walks it to the front himself. The proctor takes it without looking and drops it on a stack with an index card on top, in red ink: MARSH.
Cal doesn't know who Marsh is. On the way out he hears two girls saying the name the way people say the name of a storm.

reaction.text: CAL PRUITT. The name off a fake Vermont license, off this very building, on the one true thing. It seems funny, for about a second. Then it seems like the most honest thing he's ever done: if somebody's going to read it, let it be nobody.
The proctor doesn't check names against anything. He takes it without looking and drops it on a stack with an index card on top, in red ink: MARSH.

The proctor looks at the empty book. Then at him. Then at the empty book again.

He drops it on a stack marked MARSH. The pages stay in Cal's back pocket, warm, folded, a square of himself he can feel when he sits down.

blocks.text: INT. DOT'S DINER, MILL STREET. MORNING (WED 9:20 A.M.)

Pancakes the size of hubcaps, with a pat of butter on top like a hat. Yusuf takes his first bite and stops chewing, and closes his eyes, and doesn't open them for a while, and nobody at the table says anything, because some things are sacred.

DOT, the beehive, the reading glasses, refills Cal's coffee without asking and points at him with the pot. "The Okafor boy's friend. Grace boy." She remembers him at the table on Monday, holding Mrs. Okafor's hand, looking at the ketchup for a long time. He didn't know anyone saw that. Dot sees everything. Dot has seen forty years of Whitlock boys cry into her ketchup.

Dev is lighter today than Cal has seen him. Rested, almost glowing, in a way that makes no sense for a guy who went for a run last night in church shoes and came back at nine-fifteen. He's telling Yusuf about Houston. He's doing voices. He looks like somebody set something heavy down.
Danny Doyle is busing, pencil behind his ear, gray bin on his hip. He clocks Cal from three booths away and his face lights up like he's seen a satisfied customer, which he has.
Pruitt! How's the license working? Any problems? Any feedback? I take feedback.
Pruitt?
Cal has to produce it. There's no way out. He slides it across the Formica: CALVIN R. PRUITT, Burlington, Vermont, twenty-two years old, looking tired against a walk-in freezer door.
Burlington. You've never been to Burlington.
I've been to Burlington spiritually.
Yusuf wipes his fingers on a napkin, picks up the license by its edges and tilts it toward the window light, slowly, at three angles, like a jeweler with a loupe. The whole table watches him do it.
The hologram is a sticker.
The hologram is a premium sticker.
It catches light at forty-five degrees. A real one doesn't. A bouncer with a phone flashlight will see it.

Danny looks at Yusuf the way a young artist looks at a critic who is right. Dev puts his fork down. Under the table, Cal can feel the next ten seconds of his reputation being decided by a kid with a pencil behind his ear.

choices.label: Let Yusuf “fix” it with a napkin and his phone

reaction.text: Yusuf takes a straw, the corner of a paper napkin, a dab of Dot's maple syrup, and his phone, with an app open that shows a light meter. He works for ninety seconds without speaking. When he's done, the sticker reads as real at three angles. He hands it back without ceremony.
Who ARE you?
Nobody.

He says it flatly. He means it. He needs it to be true, and Cal, who reads people, sees how much. Danny tries to hire him on the spot, ten percent, then twenty. Yusuf declines and goes back to his pancakes. Danny writes his own phone number on Yusuf's check anyway.

choices.label: Cut it up with Dot's butter knife, right there

reaction.text: He picks up Dot's butter knife and saws the license in half on the Formica. It takes longer than you'd think. A premium sticker is a premium sticker.
That was a hundred and twenty dollars of ART.
You were very talented. It's a tribute.

Danny walks away holding the two halves like a dead bird. Dev doesn't say anything. But something in his shoulders unlocks, a quarter-inch, like a door coming off a latch, and when the check comes he pays for everyone's pancakes before Cal can even reach for his wallet, and won't discuss it.

choices.label: Ask Danny why a junior needs side money that badly

reaction.text: Can I ask you something? Why does a junior in high school need side money that badly?
Danny's grin goes flat, like a TV switched off.
Same reason as everyone in this town, chief.

He takes the bin and goes back to busing. On the way out Cal leaves a big tip under his plate, too big, the kind of tip he knows is a bribe to his own conscience. When he looks back through the window, Danny is folding the bills into a sock behind the counter. Not his apron. A sock. Something in it already. He puts the sock in his backpack and zips it.

blocks.text: Act Two · Legacy
INT. WHITAKER COMMONS, THE GRIND (COFFEE BAR). DAY (WED 11:30 A.M.)

The Grind is the coffee bar off the Commons lobby: subway tile, a chalkboard menu with puns on it, and, mounted over the espresso machine because God has a sense of humor, a second, smaller portrait of Charles Whitaker, this one smiling. Cal is in line under his grandfather's teeth when he realizes the person in front of him is Nora Castellanos.

Same thrifted blazer, sleeves shoved up. Herald lanyard. A stack of this morning's print edition under one arm, her byline face-up, MOVE-IN: WHO GETS IN?, like a calling card she's daring people to read.

She orders a large cold brew, black. Before she can tap her card, Cal reaches past her and taps his. The barista, who has the energy of a man in a hostage situation with a milk frother, doesn't care who pays. Nora turns around very slowly.
Coffee boy.
I said I'd buy you a coffee and prove you wrong. Step one.
Step one of what? Paying for things isn't a personality, it's a feature of your bank.
But she takes the cold brew. She lets him. He watches her be annoyed that she let him, which is better than the coffee.

She orders a large cold brew, black, and when he reaches past her to pay she lets him, with a look that says she's noting it. "That's not a bribe," he says. "I know," she says. "That's why I'm letting you."

She orders a large cold brew, black. When he reaches past her to pay, she slaps her own card down on the reader so hard the barista flinches, and she doesn't look at him, not once, until the coffee's in her hand. Then she does, and it's worse.
Mr. Like-the-Building. You're having a week.
She holds up her phone. A draft headline, cursor blinking: LEGACY TOAST GOES VIRAL: THE WHITAKER PROBLEM.

Your toast is at forty thousand views since that account reposted it at seven this morning. People are making it a sound. A girl in Ohio lip-synced it with a cat. My editor wants a follow-up. I want you on the record.
The chant video is at forty thousand views since that account reposted it at seven this morning. A girl in Ohio lip-synced it with a cat. My editor wants a follow-up. I want you on the record.
Also I saw you come out of placement. You looked like you'd been in a car accident. Whatever you wrote, you should frame it.
Then something he doesn't expect. She puts the phone face-down on the counter.
I'm not going to ask you about the motel. The second slide. That's not news. That's somebody's life.

She says it flatly, like a rule she wrote down a long time ago and keeps in her wallet. It's the kindest thing anyone's said to him all day, and it's from the person who wrote rich idiot under his name.
Then, too casual, stirring a coffee that has nothing in it to stir:
Does your father ever talk about the Rho? Back then, I mean. What the house was like. Fall of ninety-one, say. His junior year.

The margin of her notebook on Monday, boxed twice: SKR, fall '91, ask G.M.? He hasn't thought about it since. He thinks about it now. And under all of it is his father's 1:14 a.m. text, the one instruction his father gave him in writing: The Herald will want a legacy quote. Don't give them one.

choices.label: Go on the record: give her a real, true quote

reaction.text: You want a quote? Here. When your name's on the building, people don't see you. They see a plaque. Everybody reads the plaque and nobody reads the guy. I'd like to be read, at some point. That's all. Print it.
She writes it down without looking at the page, eyes on him the whole time. That's how he knows it's good: she doesn't need to check it.
You're going to get in trouble for that.
I'm always in trouble. This time I picked it.
She almost smiles. She converts it into a sip of cold brew at the last second, like a professional.

reaction.text: No comment.
She nods slowly, like he's confirmed something she already had from two sources.
Your father's line.
How do you know it's his line?
Everyone's father has the same line. They hand it down with the watch.

She writes four words and turns the notebook so he can read them: declined to comment. Then, underneath, smaller: paid for this reporter's coffee. He realizes she's going to print both, side by side, and that it's going to be devastating, and that it's going to be fair.

choices.label: “Is this about ‘SKR, fall '91’?”

reaction.text: Is this about "SKR, fall '91"? I read your margin. On Monday. Upside down.
For one second, Nora Castellanos is not faster than him. She goes completely still, the way she did at the tent when she put her hand over the page. Not a muscle. A deer hearing a twig.
Eyes up, Whitlock.
My eyes are up. That's the problem.
She looks at him for a long time. Then she lowers her voice under the hiss of the milk steamer, and makes him an offer like she's sliding a contract across a table.
If your father ever says anything about that year. Anything. A name, a joke, a story he tells at dinner. You tell me. And I'll owe you a coffee.
You already owe me a coffee.
Then I'll owe you two.
He doesn't know what he's just agreed to. He knows it's the first time she's needed anything from him, and that she hates it, and that she asked anyway.

She takes a Herald business card from her blazer and writes a number on the back in ballpoint, then holds out her hand for his phone, types his number into her own, and gives the card to him. Two words under the number, underlined: Tips. Not a date.

blocks.text: EXT. THE QUAD. DAY (WED 3:00 P.M.)

The Orientation Games: house versus house on the Quad, under a sky so blue it seems smug. An egg toss. A three-legged race. A Whitlock trivia round in which Simon answers every question before it's finished being asked, and Lowell is penalized for it.
Simon coaches Lowell 3 like a disgraced Olympic gymnastics coach, pacing the sideline in his camel coat with a whistle he found somewhere.
We are losing in the dignity bracket. We are losing in the fun bracket. Hunter, you're not losing, you're just ugly at it.

Priya films everything vertically, running backward along the sideline, narrating into her phone in a breathless nature-documentary whisper. She seems fine. She seems more than fine. She hasn't stopped moving since breakfast.

Priya films everything vertically, running backward along the sideline, narrating into her phone in a breathless nature-documentary whisper. Every so often she glances at Cal and then away, fast, like checking a stove.
Priya films everything vertically from the far side of the Quad, with the Thorne House team, as far from Lowell as the grass allows. She hasn't looked at him once. He's checked. He's checked a lot.

Cal and Dev win the three-legged race, ankles tied in a Whitlock bandana, by falling over the line in a heap. Dev lies on the grass laughing too hard to get up. Yusuf, keeping time, in a monotone: "Personal best."
Then the crowd parts the way crowds part for money.

Three Rho brothers in navy quarter-zips crossing the grass with the unhurried walk of people whose families own the grass. One carries a cardboard box. The red-faced one has a lacrosse stick he doesn't need.

And in front: tall, easy, sleeves pushed up, a watch so old it's almost poor. Beautiful in a way that's a little cruel to look at. He's laughing at something, and Cal hears the laugh before he sees the face, and knows it, the way you know a song from the first bar without knowing its name.
He has your father's laugh, Margaux said on Monday, on the lawn, a drink in her hand. It's unsettling.
This is BROOKS HADLEY III, 20.

blocks.name: FITZ
blocks.text: Kappa sweatshirt guy! Legend! You waved at them, dude. You waved.
Calvin Whitaker.
Your father emailed the chapter last night. Two sentences. "My son will be rushing. Make him welcome." He's never written me more than one.
Your father called me last night. Late. He sounded upset, which I didn't know he could do. He says you'll be rushing anyway.
Your father's assistant emailed me your class schedule. Unprompted. Charming. I know you have Intro to Econ at nine on Tuesdays and that you'll skip it.
He holds out a hand. Cal shakes it. It's dry and warm and very firm, and he holds on half a second too long, like he's taking a pulse.
"The most Whitaker sentence ever spoken." I've been trying to say that for three years. You said it in one night, standing on a folding table. It's honestly upsetting.
Behind Cal, Simon has stopped coaching. He's watching Brooks with an expression Cal's never seen on him, one without a joke in it.

Brooks takes a small leather notebook out of his back pocket, the kind with an elastic band, and a short pencil, like a golf pencil. He opens it. Then he asks, friendly, like it's nothing, like it's the weather:
Can you swim?

It's not an answer. It's the shape of an answer, with nothing inside it, like a box with the presents taken out.

blocks.text: EXT. THE QUAD, BY THE LOWELL TEAM TABLE. CONTINUOUS (3:15 P.M.)
The brother with the box sets it on Lowell's folding table, on top of the egg cartons. Navy Rho quarter-zips, embroidered crest, folded like flags. Brooks lifts one out and shakes it open.
Legacies only. House rule. Which on Lowell 3 means you, Whitaker, and nobody else. Congratulations. It's a small club and the dues are your personality.
He hands it over. Then he looks up past Cal at Lowell House, at the third floor, at the bay window over the Quad with the Commons sign reflected in it.
Daddy's single. Bay window. Fireplace. I lived in a Lowell closet freshman year. Fourth floor. They put a bed where the brooms go. My father doesn't make calls.
It's a joke, and it lands like one, and the brothers laugh. But there's something under it Cal can hear, a grievance with real weight, like a stone in a sock.

Dev, at the table, already knows the single was a call. Cal told him yesterday. Brooks just confirmed it, in public, out loud, and Dev doesn't look surprised. He looks at Cal with something like sympathy, which is worse.
Lottery.
Secret lottery.
Dev, at the table, doesn't look at Cal. The lottery is right there between them, in the grass, and Brooks just kicked it.
Then Brooks turns to Dev, who's holding the carton of leftover eggs, and smiles at him with every tooth.
And you're the double. Lowell's charity suite. They keep one room for the scholarship kids so the brochure has range.

Dev's jaw sets. Cal has never seen Dev angry. He almost sees it now: a flicker, a muscle in the cheek, the hand on the egg carton going very still. Then it's put away, folded and filed. Dev smiles back. It's a terrifying smile, because it's so nice.
Cal hears himself ask it, before he decides to.
Do you know my father well?
Barely. He's a name on an email.
And Brooks rubs his left eyebrow with his thumb. Left side. Thumb. Like a man checking his hairline is still there.
Cal's own tell, which Simon named for him on a staircase yesterday. On another man's face. He goes cold in the sun. He doesn't know what he's looking at. He knows he's looking at something.
He says you've given your word. In this house, a word is a contract.

Brooks produces a heavy cream card from his back pocket, the kind of stock you can feel the money in, and tucks it into the folded quarter-zip in Cal's hands. Engraved, black ink: SIGMA KAPPA RHO. LEGACY DINNER. THURSDAY, EIGHT O'CLOCK. THE CHAPTER ROOM. SONS ONLY.
Dev is still holding the eggs.

choices.label: Laugh it off, take the quarter-zip

reaction.text: He laughs. The easy one, the one that keeps rooms on his side, the one he's used at every table his father ever sat him at. It comes out perfect. It always does.
There he is.
Dev picks up the egg carton and walks back to the Lowell side of the table without a word. He takes his place in the egg toss. He catches every egg. He doesn't drop one.
Later, at dinner, Dev is completely normal. He tells a story about his sister. He passes the hot sauce. He's normal all night. That's worse.

choices.label: Cut back: “Bold talk from a man in a quarter-zip.”

reaction.text: Bold talk from a man in a quarter-zip. You look like a regional manager at a boat dealership.

Even the Rho brothers laugh. Fitz actually yelps. Brooks laughs hardest of all, genuinely, the laugh, head back, and when he comes out of it he's looking at Cal with something like recognition, like a man spotting his own handwriting on someone else's envelope.
Oh, you're going to be fun.
He means it as a threat and a compliment, and Cal means his the same way, and they both know it. Dev, holding the eggs, says nothing. But he's smiling at the carton.

choices.label: “He carried my boxes. You carried a box of sweaters.”

reaction.text: He carried my boxes up three flights on Monday. Unasked. You carried a box of sweaters across a lawn and made a guy hold it.

No joke to hide behind. The Quad goes a little quiet around them, the way it does around a dropped tray. Brooks's smile stays exactly where it is, not a millimeter of movement, and that's how Cal knows it hit.
Loyal. Your father wasn't.

He leaves the card in the quarter-zip anyway, on the table, on top of the eggs, and walks off with his brothers. Dev says nothing for a long moment. Then he bumps Cal's shoulder with his own, once, hard enough to almost put him into the egg table, and leaves his shoulder there a second longer than a bump needs.

blocks.text: INT. CAL'S SINGLE, LOWELL HOUSE. EVENING (WED 8:40 P.M.)

Cal on his mattress, which is still on the floor, because he didn't build a loft and doesn't intend to. The Rho quarter-zip is on the floorboards in a heap where he dropped it. The cream card is on his desk, propped against Winterkill and Kevin the skull, who look at it with matching skepticism.
Two texts arrive inside the same five seconds, like they've coordinated.

Bring my sweatshirt. Don't be seen bringing my sweatshirt.

blocks.text: Right side out, please.

I have wine and opinions, and one of the opinions is about you.

blocks.text: And a third, from PRIYA (EMERGENCIES + VIBES), the first since this morning: no words, just a photo. Gerald, the radiator, shot from below, lit by a phone flashlight like a monument. A peace offering, or a threat. He can't tell. He's been unable to tell with her all day.
Gerald bangs, once, like a man clearing his throat at a funeral.

choices.label: The Kappa back stairs. Bring the sweatshirt.

reaction.text: He finds the sweatshirt, smells it, which he would deny under oath, and shoves it into a Whitlock Bookstore bag so it looks bought.

choices.label: Simon's room. Wine and opinions.

reaction.text: He texts Margaux: can't tonight. sorry. It's delivered. It's read. Read 8:44 PM. Nothing comes back, which is its own kind of sentence. He puts on his shoes and goes to drink wine with a poet.

blocks.text: EXT. KAPPA LAMBDA HOUSE, BACK SERVICE STAIRS. DUSK (WED 9:00 P.M.)

The back of the Kappa house is where the money stops pretending. An iron service staircase painted black so many times it's soft. A dumpster. A recycling bin full of champagne bottles. Beyond the hedges, past the backyards of Elm Row, the lake is a darker stripe under a sky that's gone the blue of a gas flame.

Margaux is sitting on the fourth step from the top in black leggings and his St. Anselm's swim parka, the crest on the chest, the sleeves past her fingertips. She doesn't seem to notice she's wearing it. Or she's decided not to.
I meant both, by the way. Request and warning. I always mean both.

He hands her the bookstore bag. She looks inside, at her own sweatshirt, and sets it on the step beside her, and doesn't give him back the parka, and neither of them mentions it. It's like a treaty nobody's signed.

She's funnier in the dark. Faster. Less perfect, around the edges, like a drawing before it's inked. She does four minutes on the Kappa freshman brunch, which she calls "a hostage situation with mimosas," and he laughs out loud, and she shushes him, and then she laughs too.
Your diary's very popular. I saw it at the brunch. Twelve sisters reading your trauma over egg-white omelets. One of them cried. She's a Pisces.
Then, lightly:
Nobody knows. Still?
She reads it on his face before he can answer. His reads don't work on her. Hers work on him.
Who.
Priya. She found the sweatshirt. She swore on a skull.
A long beat. Margaux looks at the lake. Her face does nothing, which costs her something.
Then it's Priya's problem now.
Still. Nobody.
Still. Nobody. A girl on my floor thinks I'm a sorority superfan.
Aren't you?

She pulls the parka tighter. Then, almost against her will, like it's being pulled out of her on a string: "You told me the truth about him. On the lawn. People don't do that with me. They tell me what I want." "What do you want?" "Not that," she says. "Something worse."
And then, the same light voice, the same careless angle of the head, like it's just what you ask a boy on a staircase:
Is your father coming up for Convocation? Does he sit with the trustees, or does he do that thing where he stands at the back so people have to turn around?

Again. The calendar. A list somebody gave her. And as she reaches up to push her hair out of her face, he sees the outside edge of her right hand: a long smear of graphite, from the little finger down to the wrist, silver-gray, the way a person's hand goes when they've been drawing for hours, dragging it across the page.

choices.label: “You've been drawing.” Take her hand and look.

reaction.text: He takes her right hand and turns it over, palm up, in the light from the kitchen window. She lets him. That surprises both of them.
You've been drawing.
A long pause. The dumpster hums.

Fennimore has the original Whitlock plans in Special Collections. 1791. Ink on linen. They got the chapel wrong. The proportions. It's been wrong for two hundred and thirty-five years and nobody's noticed. I was fixing it.
It's the most she has ever said to him. More than on the roof. It comes out fast, like she's afraid it'll stop.
Then she takes her hand back and wipes it on her leggings.
Don't make it a thing.
He doesn't. He walks home along Elm Row with it anyway, the graphite, the chapel, a thing.

choices.label: “He told me to wear the navy suit for Convocation.”

reaction.text: He told me to wear the navy suit for Convocation. That's all I know. That's the most he's told me about anything since March.

It's the only real thing he knows about his father's plans, and he gives it to her like a gift, because she asked, and because she's cold, and because he wants to see her face when he gives her something.

She absorbs it completely. He watches it go in. And something in her shoulders lets go, like a coat coming off a hook. She leans over and kisses his cheek, briefly, correctly, the kind of kiss you give a doorman at Christmas.
Thank you.
He feels useful. He walks home feeling useful. He doesn't know what for.
EXT. KAPPA BACK STAIRS. MOMENTS LATER
Margaux alone on the iron steps in his parka. She takes out her phone. MOM. She types without hesitating.

msgs.text: Navy suit. Convocation. He's coming.

reaction.text: Three dots. Then:

msgs.text: Good girl.

reaction.text: Margaux reads it. She puts the phone in the parka pocket and keeps her hand there, around it, for a long time, the way you'd hold a stone you were deciding whether to throw.

choices.label: Kiss her on the stairs before she asks anything else

reaction.text: He kisses her before she can ask anything else. Against the iron railing, the parka bunched in his hands, her back to the cold metal. She kisses back hard, harder than on the roof, like she's been thinking about it all day and is annoyed about that.
Then she pushes him off with one hand flat on his chest, firm, the way you'd stop a door.
Not here. Not in the light. Go home, Whitaker.
She's smiling. She's also, he notices, checking the windows above them, every one of them, left to right, the way you'd count exits.

blocks.text: INT. SIMON'S ROOM, THORNE HOUSE. NIGHT (WED 9:00 P.M.)

Thorne House is the sophomore dorm, and Simon's single is on the fourth floor under the eaves. Every wall is papered floor to ceiling with poems torn out of library books, overlapping like fish scales. Anne Carson. Frank O'Hara. A signed photo of Fran Lebowitz glaring from over the bed. A framed rejection slip from The Paris Review, hung like a diploma.
The "ailment council" is just the two of them. Cheap Lillet in very good glasses, crystal, heavy, clearly stolen from a wedding.
My mother's. From her wedding. She doesn't know I have them. She doesn't know a lot. It's how we stay close.

Simon is the best company on campus, and he knows it, and he works for it anyway. Gossip as anthropology. He gives Cal the whole map. The dean of students wears bow ties "as a form of apology." The a cappella group that is legally a church. Margaux Vance and Brooks Hadley, "on, off, on, like a lighthouse warning ships." The Rho president, Hollis Prescott: "A senator's grandson with the soul of a golden retriever. Kind. Square. Smells like cedar."
He says the name Hollis very carefully. Too carefully. Like someone carrying a full glass across a room.
Don't do the thing. You did it on the stairs. If you read me again tonight I'll cry, and I'm a very ugly crier. I go red in patches. Like a map of Europe.

He picks up where he left off on Margaux, unprompted: "She tutors, you know. Calculus. For money. In Fennimore, in the carrels, where she thinks nobody goes." Cal pretends not to care. Simon looks at his face and says, "Eyebrow," and refills his glass.
And can we toast your comment? "It's fiction, buy the book." I'd buy the book. I'd buy two and leave one on a train.
Then Simon looks into the ice bucket, which is empty, and swears in what sounds like Dutch.
Ice. Don't touch anything. Especially don't touch anything.

He goes out. His footsteps go down the hall. And there on the desk, in reach, under a library copy of Plath's Ariel with the due-date card still in it from 1988, is a manila folder. Labeled in fountain pen, in a neat, slanting hand:

His father's initials. On a poet's desk. Under Ariel. Cal sits very still with a glass of Lillet in his hand and listens to an ice machine down the hall, which sounds, of course, like someone choking.

choices.label: Open it while he's getting ice

reaction.text: He opens it. Two things.

A color printout, pixelated: a ballroom, a banner, WHITAKER LYLE · HAPPY HOLIDAYS 2006, and his father, younger, black tie, mid-laugh, head back, a glass in one hand. His father laughing. Cal can't remember seeing it in person.
Beside it, a photo of Cal. Yesterday. The stairwell. Wavy light on his face. The ailments chart.

Footsteps. He shuts the folder and puts Ariel back on top and is leaning back in his chair with his glass when Simon comes in with a bowl of ice. Simon sets it down. He looks at the desk. The folder has moved a quarter of an inch. Cal can see him see it.
Neither of them says anything. The rest of the night is very funny and very careful, like two people dancing around a hole in the floor.

choices.label: Ask him straight out when he's back

reaction.text: Simon comes back with the ice. Cal waits until he's sitting down.
What's R.W. '06?
Simon doesn't miss a beat. He doesn't even glance at the desk.
My mother's tax documents. She's a secretary in Back Bay. R.W. is her accountant. Ronald Wexler. Very glamorous man. Toupee.
Then he drinks. For a long time. He drinks until the glass is empty, and then he looks into the empty glass like there might be more at the bottom, and there isn't.
It's the first time Cal has seen Simon Achterberg without a next line.

choices.label: Leave it. Ask him about Hollis instead.

reaction.text: He leaves the folder alone. When Simon comes back with the ice, Cal waits until he's sitting.
You said Hollis like it costs you money.
Silence. Simon puts two cubes in each glass, one at a time, with his fingers, very precisely.
You're horrible. Drink your Lillet.

He doesn't deny it. He doesn't confirm it. A door closes between them, gently, with a click. And another one opens somewhere else in the house, and they both hear it, and they sit in the draft and drink, and talk about Anne Carson until two.

blocks.text: INT. CAL'S SINGLE, LOWELL HOUSE. EVENING (THU 08-27, 7:40 P.M.)

Thursday was a blur: a floor meeting about the account that June ran like a hostage negotiator, a library tour, a consent lecture with a puppet. The account posted twice more, small things. 1,100 followers. It hasn't touched Cal again. That's somehow worse.
Now it's 7:40, and he is half into the navy suit.
His father's suit, effectively. Ordered by Denise in June, delivered in a garment bag with a card in a hand very close to his father's: For Convocation. He's wearing it two weeks early.

msgs.text: Brooks says Thursday.
Wear the jacket.

Sent at 6:02 p.m. He has read it eleven times. Under it, an email, which arrived at 6:15 with the efficiency of a train schedule.

From: Denise Farrow. Subject: Rush calendar! "Hi Cal! Attached: the Sigma Kappa Rho rush calendar for September 3–18. Your father asks that you attend tonight's dinner. Also, no mail for you this week! I'll forward anything that comes, as always. No worries if you're busy! —D."
No worries if you're busy. His own words, from the back of a car on Monday, handed back to him in someone else's mouth. He wonders if she knows she does it. He suspects she knows everything.
The card is on his desk against Winterkill. SONS ONLY. He picks up the tie.
Then a knock. Not a knock: a rhythm, knocked by several people who didn't agree on the rhythm.

He opens the door. Simon, in a headlamp, the camel coat, a canvas tote. Dev, with a big yellow flashlight and a Ziploc of granola bars "for morale and blood sugar." Yusuf, with his laptop open in both hands like a waiter with a tray, the screen showing a scanned blueprint: WHITLOCK UNIVERSITY STEAM DISTRIBUTION · 1974.
And Priya, behind them, in a yellow plastic miner's helmet with a working light, holding a bottle of something blue. "I've come as a canary," she says. "If I die, run."

And Priya, behind them, in a yellow plastic miner's helmet with a working light, holding a bottle of something blue. She grins at him, a little too wide, and doesn't quite meet his eyes. "I've come as a canary. If I die, run."
No Priya. Dev, reading his face: "She said she'll meet us there. She said, quote, if Columbo comes, tell him I'm wearing a wire."
Anti-Orientation. The real Whitlock. Under it, through it, over it. We leave in four minutes. Bring a jacket you don't love.
Simon looks at the navy suit. He looks at it for a long time, like he's trying to memorize the line of the shoulder.
Although that one's lovely.
No pressure, man. Your call.
A degree cooler than Dev usually is. Dev doesn't look at the Rho quarter-zip on the floor, so carefully it's the only thing in the room.
No pressure, man. Your call. Seriously.
No pressure, man. Your call. Seriously. And for the record, I'd understand. It's your dad.
The card on the desk. The suit on his shoulders. Proud of you on the screen in his hand, still lit. Four people in his doorway, one of them in a headlamp. Gerald says nothing. Even Gerald is waiting.

choices.label: Button the jacket. Go to the Legacy Dinner.

reaction.text: He buttons the jacket. Middle button only, the way he was taught at eight by a tailor on Newbury Street. It's a very small sound.
I'm sorry. I told him I would. Next time. I swear.

Simon looks at him with an expression that is almost proud and almost heartbroken, and says, "Of course," and means both. Dev nods and says "Next time," and holds out a granola bar, and Cal takes it, and puts it in the pocket of his father's suit.

choices.label: Take off the jacket. Go under the school.

reaction.text: He takes off the jacket. He hangs it on the back of his door, on the hook, the way it came, the way it'll wait. He puts the cream card face-down on the desk.
Give me a jacket I don't love.

Dev throws him a Houston Astros hoodie from across the hall. Simon claps once, the gavel. Yusuf closes his laptop. And for the first time since Monday, Cal leaves his phone on the desk, face-down, beside the card, and then goes back for it, because he's not that person yet.

blocks.text: Act Three · Sons Only
INT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO HOUSE, FOYER AND CHAPTER ROOM. NIGHT (THU 8:00 P.M.)

The Rho smells like what it is: leather, lemon oil, wet stone, and a century of cigar smoke soaked so deep into the velvet curtains it's structural. A double staircase. A moose head in a lacrosse pinnie. Over the archway, a banner: WELCOME HOME LEGACYS.
At the door FITZ, the red-faced one from the Quad, in a pink tie, is carding freshmen with a flashlight.

blocks.name: FITZ
blocks.text: ID. ID, please. Tradition! It's a tradition.
Cal's hand comes out of his wallet with the Vermont license before his brain is consulted. Before Fitz can squint at it, a hand reaches over his shoulder and plucks it away.
Brooks tilts it to the chandelier, the way Yusuf did at Dot's, and his mouth goes up at one corner.
Dot's laminator. The kid's an artist.
Somebody's improved the hologram, though. Interesting. That's not his work.
He hands it back with a wink. Cal doesn't know how Brooks knows whose laminator it was, and knows better than to ask on the front steps.
I don't have an ID. I had a very premium one. It died.

blocks.name: FITZ
blocks.text: Rookie.
Get another. Dot's diner. Ask for the busboy. Tell him I sent you; he'll give you the house rate.
I don't have an ID on me.

blocks.name: FITZ
blocks.text: Rookie.
