The chapter room. A long table, candles in silver, eight freshmen in jackets that cost more than some cars, two pledges in white waiter's jackets serving steak nobody wants. Oil portraits of the 1890 founders. A silver loving cup the size of a toddler.
The president sends his regrets. He's at a senators' thing. There's always a senators' thing. So you get me.
The ritual: each legacy stands and says his father's name and class year, and the room says it back. A roll call. A liturgy.

blocks.name: TEDDY PEMBERTON
blocks.paren: standing, soft-faced, too much hair gel
blocks.text: Edward Pemberton. '96.

blocks.name: ROOM
blocks.text: Edward Pemberton, '96.
Teddy sits fast. Everyone in America knows the name Edward Pemberton this year; it's been on cable news since March, next to the word indicted.

blocks.name: FRESHMAN 2
blocks.text: Charles Lindgren. '01.

blocks.name: ROOM
blocks.text: Charles Lindgren, '01.
Brooks takes his own turn flat, like reading a serial number off a part.
Brooks Hadley the Third. Son of Brooks Hadley Junior. The room knows the year.
And then, before Cal can stand, Brooks lifts the cup himself and turns it toward him.
Calvin Whitaker. Son of Richard Whitaker, '93. Pledge master.

blocks.name: ROOM
blocks.text: Richard Whitaker, '93.
His father's name, said back to him by strangers in unison. It does something to his spine.
And now, because it's on the internet and we're a modern house: the sequel.
Brooks raises his glass. The room quiets. He looks right at Cal, smiling, easy.
The legacy toast. Make it funny at someone else's expense.
Next time make it funny at someone else's expense. His father's text, 1:14 a.m., Monday night, word for word. Not paraphrased. The same eight words, in the same order, in another man's mouth.
Brooks, passing behind his chair, low: "Your friend from the charity suite isn't invited. You'll notice."
Eight boys turn to look at him. Teddy Pemberton is looking at his steak.

choices.label: Roast Teddy Pemberton and his father's indictment

reaction.text: He reads Teddy in one glance, the way he reads everyone: the gel, the bitten thumbnail, the way he flinched when the room said his father's name. He goes for the softest place, because it's right there, and because his father asked him to.

To Teddy Pemberton. The only man at this table whose father can't make it to Parents' Weekend for legal reasons. Teddy, when they ask you to stand for your father's name, it's not a toast. It's a sentencing.
The room screams. Fists on the table. A pledge in a white jacket drops a fork. Teddy laughs along with everybody, louder than everybody, and his eyes are wet, and he keeps laughing.
At the head of the table, Brooks watches Cal with an expression Cal can't name. It could be pride. It could be grief. It might be the same thing, on him.
There he is.

choices.label: Roast Brooks: the quarter-zips, the notebook, the swimming

reaction.text: To our pledge master. A man who asked me today if I could swim, wrote down the answer in a leather notebook with a golf pencil, and then handed me a sweater. Brooks, I don't know what the Rho is, but I know it's the only cult with a merchandise table.
It's very funny. The room isn't sure it's allowed to laugh. Eight boys freeze, forks up, and look at Brooks. Brooks lets the silence hang for one long second.
Then he laughs, first, loud, head back. That laugh. The room explodes after him, relieved, like a dam going.
Later, passing behind Cal's chair, Brooks bends close to his ear, still smiling, and says it so quietly it's almost tender:
You get one. That was it.

choices.label: Toast “everyone whose father came by email”

reaction.text: To our fathers. Who came tonight the way they always come. By email. By check. By portrait. To Edward Pemberton, who's busy. To Charles Lindgren, who's in Singapore. To Richard Whitaker, who sent me a text at six o'clock that said wear the jacket. I'm wearing the jacket. To the jackets.
It's funny, and it's true, and it's the first time some of these boys have ever heard it said out loud. The room goes silent. Nobody knows what to do with their face.
Then Teddy Pemberton starts clapping. Slowly, alone, his eyes very bright. Then the boy next to him. Then all of them, standing, clapping for their fathers' absence like it's a team they're on.
Brooks doesn't clap. Brooks drinks, all of it, and sets the glass down very gently, and looks at the candles.

blocks.text: INT. RHO HOUSE, THE COMPOSITE HALLWAY. NIGHT (THU 10:15 P.M.)
After dinner Brooks walks him down the back hall alone, past a coat room, past a bathroom with a framed photograph of Gerald Ford inside it, into the composite hallway. A docent in his own museum.

A century of class photos, floor to ceiling, framed in identical black: rows of ovals, boys in the same navy blazer in every one of them, from sepia to Kodachrome to digital, like one boy aging and refusing to age. The overhead lights are old brass sconces. The glass on every frame shines like water.
The wall. Every brother since 1891. Find your grandfather sometime. He looks like he's about to buy the photographer.

And then the one Brooks has clearly been walking toward the whole time. SIGMA KAPPA RHO · 1991–1992. Thirty-five ovals. Second row, center: RICHARD WHITAKER. Junior. Impossibly handsome. Jaw like a drawing of a jaw. And under the name, a little brass plate with two words: PLEDGE MASTER.

Brooks stands in front of it a little too long. Cal steps up beside him, and for one second, in the glass, there are two faces reflected over his father's photograph: his own, and Brooks's, and his father's young face between them, behind the glass, like a coin under ice.
Brooks taps an oval in the top row, without looking at it. "That's mine. My father. Look how happy." Then his hand drops.
And in the bottom row, the pledge class, there's a hole.

One oval with no photograph in it. Just green felt, faded where the light has hit it for thirty-five years. The little brass nameplate under it has been pried off with something, a screwdriver, a knife, leaving two screw holes and a fragment, still screwed in on the left side, two letters and a period: T. C
House ghost. Freshmen always ask. Ask me sometime.
His thumb goes to his left eyebrow.
Cal's phone buzzes in his jacket. 10:31 p.m.

msgs.text: Brooks says you were a credit to the name tonight.

blocks.text: Brooks is standing right there, two feet away, under his father's photograph, typing on his own phone with one thumb. He doesn't look up. He doesn't hide it.

choices.label: Photograph the empty oval while Brooks watches

reaction.text: Cal lifts his phone and takes a picture of the empty oval and the two letters. The fake shutter sound is very loud in the hallway.

Brooks watches him do it. He doesn't stop him. He doesn't say don't. He just watches, the way you'd watch a man pick up a book you put out on a table for him, which is stranger than stopping him, much stranger.
Collector.
A pause. Brooks looks at the photograph of Richard Whitaker.
Like him.

choices.label: “I'm asking. Who was T. C.?”
choices.remember: Brooks will remember that you asked.

reaction.text: I'm asking. You said ask you sometime. Who was T. C.?
A boy who couldn't swim.
It drops into the hallway like a glass. A beat, a long one.
Then Brooks laughs. The laugh. Head back.
Joking. God, your face. He dropped out. Transferred. Something boring. Every house has a ghost; ours is a guy who went to Tufts.

His thumb on his left eyebrow. Cal sees it. He has no idea what he's seeing. He's seen it twice now on someone else, and every time on himself, and the hallway feels like it's tilting very slowly toward the lake.

choices.label: “You text my father a lot.”

reaction.text: You text my father a lot.
Brooks doesn't even look up from the phone.
Somebody has to.
It's a joke. It's delivered as a joke, with the timing of a joke. It's also the saddest sentence Cal has heard anyone say this week, and that includes the internet.
Brooks pockets the phone. He claps Cal on the back, once, between the shoulder blades.
Come on. One more stop. Every legacy does it. Bring your jacket; it's cold by the water.

blocks.text: EXT. THE RHO DOCK, TAMSIN LAKE. NIGHT (THU 11:40 P.M.)

Down the back lawn of the Rho, past a boat shed with a padlock on it and a canoe on sawhorses, through a gap in the hedge, to the house's private dock. Old gray boards, some newer than others. A single bare bulb on a post, haloed with moths. Beyond it, black water, all the way to the far shore, where the boathouse light is a pinprick, like a star someone dropped.

It's the first time Cal has been to the lake. Three days on campus and he's seen it from every window, from the bay, from the crest of Route 7, and it's the first time he's stood on it. It's colder than he thought. It's bigger.

Brooks produces a bottle of Stoli from the inside of his jacket. They pass it back and forth, sitting at the end of the dock, feet over the water. The boards are wet. Somewhere out on the lake there's a buoy, white, a hundred yards off, nodding on nothing.

Brooks is different out here. Quieter. He talks about the house the way a person talks about a parent: a little contempt, a lot of need, a joke where the feeling should be. The roof leaks. The founders were frauds. He loves it. He'd burn it down.
Every legacy stands here once. Your father stood right here. On this board, probably. So did mine.
He says it to the water, not to Cal.
Neither of them mentions the toast. It's out here with them anyway, like a third person on the dock.

Then he stands and takes a flashlight out of his jacket and clicks it on under his chin, like a camp counselor telling a ghost story to eleven-year-olds, and he's grinning, bright, and the grin doesn't touch his eyes at all.
Prove you can swim, Whitaker. Out to the buoy and back.
Two-hundred free. Show me.
A very handsome stone, you said. Let's see you sink.
Only toward money, you said. There's a dollar on the buoy. I swear.
It's tradition.

choices.label: Strip to his boxers and dive

reaction.text: He takes off his father's jacket and folds it on the boards. Shoes. Shirt. Trousers. The cold air on his skin like a slap. Brooks holds the flashlight on him the whole time, steady, like a spotlight on a stage.
Then he dives.

The cold stops his heart. That's what it feels like: a hand closing on it. Everything goes silent and black and enormous. No sound but his own blood, thudding in his ears, slow, slower. For one second he doesn't know which way is up. For one second it's very peaceful, and that scares him more than the cold.

Then his body remembers St. Anselm's before he does. The catch, the pull, the breath every third stroke. He comes up swimming. Buoy, a hundred yards of black water, his arms finding the old rhythm like a language he forgot he spoke. He slaps the buoy. It's slimy. He turns. He comes back, fast, clean, faster than he's swum since junior year.

When he hauls himself up onto the boards, gasping, steaming in the cold, Brooks is standing at the very edge of the dock with the flashlight in his hand, and the beam is shaking. Not a lot. Enough. And he's not grinning anymore.
Good.
Then, almost to himself:
Now you know the water.
He tosses Cal his shirt and walks up the lawn toward the house without waiting, without looking back, the flashlight off, a dark shape getting smaller.

choices.label: “I'm not your pledge yet, Hadley.”

reaction.text: I'm not your pledge yet, Hadley.
Brooks laughs, and it's a real one, for once, surprised out of him.
Yet.

He lets it go. Easily. Too easily. He clicks off the flashlight and sits back down and hands Cal the bottle, and they finish the Stoli with their feet hanging over the black water, talking about nothing: boarding schools, terrible coaches, the best way to fake sick at Christmas. For ten minutes it's almost friendship. It's almost something else, something Cal doesn't have a word for.
When they stand up to go, Brooks looks at the buoy for a long time.

reaction.text: You first, Hadley. You're the pledge master. Show me how it's done.
He holds out the bottle. Brooks freezes.

One second. Less. But his hand on the flashlight goes white at the knuckles, and the beam drops off Cal's face and onto the black water, and stays there, shaking very slightly, like it's looking for something.
I don't swim at night.
Then he's himself again, all at once, cruel and bright, the switch thrown.
That's what pledges are for.

But Cal saw it. Real fear. Not performed, not managed, not dressed up as a joke. The only unperformed thing he has seen on Brooks Hadley's face. He doesn't know what to do with it, so he does what he always does with something he can't use yet. He files it.

EXT. BEHIND FENNIMORE LIBRARY / INT. STEAM TUNNELS UNDER THE QUAD. NIGHT (THU 9:00 P.M.)

Behind Fennimore, between a dumpster and a hedge that hasn't been trimmed since the Clinton administration, there's an iron grate set into a concrete apron in the ground, marked WHITLOCK PHYSICAL PLANT · NO ENTRY · DANGER. Yusuf crouches over it. He slides his library card into a seam at the edge, does something small with his wrist, looks at the lock in a way that seems personal, and the grate lifts.
How did you do that?
It wasn't locked. It was just closed.
That's the most Midwestern sentence I've ever heard.

A ladder. Then the tunnels: brick vaults just tall enough to walk in if you're not Dev, who walks in a permanent apology. Hot, wet air like a mouth. Pipes along both walls wrapped in old canvas, ticking and knocking as the steam moves through them, like a building full of clocks. Water drips. Somewhere far off, a pump breathes.

And the walls are written on, sixty years of it in the beam of Simon's headlamp. CLASS OF '71 AGAINST THE WAR. A dean drawn as a pig in a mortarboard. K.L. + S.K.R. = 4EVER, and under it, in a different hand, LIAR. A 413 phone number from 1983 that Dev, against all advice, calls; it's disconnected; he's devastated.

Priya arrives eight minutes late, alone, through a different grate behind the chemistry building, in a miner's helmet with a dead battery. She stands at the far end of the tunnel from Cal, as far as the brick allows, and films the walls, and doesn't film him.
Priya films everything, the miner's helmet light bobbing, narrating in a tour-guide whisper. She's holding Cal's sleeve in the dark like a kid on a field trip.
Priya films everything, the miner's helmet light bobbing, narrating in a tour-guide whisper. She stays close to Cal in the dark. Not touching. Close.

Simon conducts the whole thing in a tour-guide voice, walking backward, headlamp swinging. "On your left, the original Whitlock sin. On your right, a mural representing the death of irony, 1994." Dev laughs so hard at the tour-guide voice he has to sit down on a pipe, and leaps up instantly, because it's a steam pipe, and is fine, and laughs harder, holding his butt, tears in his eyes.
And low on one wall, near the floor, almost under the drip, old black paint gone gray and furred with damp, in plain block capitals, smaller than everything around it:
THE LAKE KEEPS.

Nobody knows what it means. Simon makes up four things it means in under a minute: a rowing slogan, a breakup line, a medieval curse, "a very bleak Yelp review." Everybody laughs. Cal laughs. He looks at it longer than the jokes need.
Simon reaches into his tote and pulls out a can of spray paint, matte black, and tosses it underhand. Cal catches it.
Every Anti-Orientee leaves a line. It's a house rule. I made it up an hour ago, but it's very old.

reaction.text: He shakes the can, the ball bearing clacking like a rattlesnake, and paints it in big confident capitals across a clean stretch of brick: CAL PRUITT WAS HERE.
Who is Cal Pruitt?
A better man.
He's not, though. He's from Burlington. He's twenty-two and he's tired. I've seen his ID.
RIP Cal Pruitt. Killed by butter knife. Gone too soon.
He's not, though. Whoever he is. I can tell.
He's not, though. Whoever he is. I can tell.

The bit is born right there in the tunnel, the way the best ones are: from now on, anything that goes wrong is Cal Pruitt's fault. Who drank the last of Simon's thermos? Pruitt. Who called the disconnected number? Pruitt. Yusuf, deadpan, eight minutes later, after a pipe hisses at them: "Pruitt."

reaction.text: He crouches by the drip, next to the old black letters, and paints small, low, careful, the can hissing, like writing on a page.
I HAVE BEEN VERY CAREFUL ABOUT TELEPHONES EVER SINCE. The last line of the essay he wrote this morning, the one somebody named Marsh is going to read.
That's new. That's raw. That's still bleeding.
MY FATHER SENDS CARS THE WAY OTHER MEN SEND FLOWERS. A line from page forty of a notebook nobody's read. It looks very small down here. It looks true.
MY FATHER SENDS CARS THE WAY OTHER MEN SEND FLOWERS. A line from page forty of a notebook nobody's read. It looks very small down here. It looks true.

Simon reads it and doesn't make a joke. Not one. He just nods, slowly, and puts his hand flat on the brick beside it for a second, like a man touching a gravestone. From Simon, that's a standing ovation.
And behind them, Priya lifts her phone and photographs it. The flash goes off in the tunnel like a gunshot. Everyone jumps. She says sorry. She doesn't delete it.

choices.label: Don't paint. Photograph THE LAKE KEEPS.

reaction.text: He doesn't add anything. He tosses the can back to Simon, crouches by the drip, and takes a photograph of the old black letters with his phone's flash. THE LAKE KEEPS, overexposed, the brick around it gone white. He doesn't know why he wants it. He wants it.
Abstaining. How Episcopal of you.
Yusuf crouches next to him. He touches the edge of the paint with one fingertip, looks at it in his phone light, smells it, which no one has ever seen a person do to graffiti.
That paint's older than the others. Lead-based. Eighties, nineties. They stopped selling it.
He stands up and wipes his finger on his hoodie and doesn't say anything else, and Cal doesn't ask, and they both look at the letters for a second longer than anybody else does.

blocks.text: INT. MARLOWE THEATER, STAGE AND FLY LOFT. NIGHT (THU 10:20 P.M.)
The tunnel ends at a ladder, and the ladder ends at a trapdoor, and the trapdoor, when Yusuf pushes it up, opens onto the stage of the Marlowe Theater.

Ghost light. A single bare bulb on a pole, center stage, the way theaters leave one burning so nobody falls into the pit in the dark. Rows and rows of empty red velvet seats going back into black. It smells like sawdust and old perfume and the inside of a piano.

Simon walks straight downstage to the apron and does Ophelia's mad scene to eight hundred empty seats, flowers and all, rosemary for remembrance, his voice going all the way to the back and coming back changed. He's good. He's very good. He's better than he'd ever let anyone tell him.
And Priya climbs.

Up the steel ladder on the stage-left wall, rung after rung, barefoot, her sneakers kicked off on the stage like two dropped commas. Up to the fly gallery. Then out, off the gallery, onto the catwalk: a steel grid walkway forty feet above the stage, no rail on one side, the ropes and pipes of the fly system hanging around her like a forest.
She walks out to the middle. She lets go of the rope. She puts her arms out. Filming herself with one hand, vertically, the phone light on her face.
I'm FLYING. Cal! Cal, look! I'm a LIGHTING CUE!

She's laughing. Her voice is too fast, the words running into each other. Even from forty feet down, in the ghost light, Cal can see her pupils are huge. He thinks of an orange pill bottle with someone else's name on it. R. MENON. He thinks of a granola bar still in its wrapper on her desk.

Dev has gone gray. Not pale: gray. He's gripping the back of a seat in the front row with both hands, his knuckles standing up like stones, and he isn't watching Priya, he's watching her hands, the way you'd watch someone's hands at a stove. His lips are moving. Cal can't hear what he's saying. It might be counting.
That's not load-rated for a person.
The catwalk sways. An inch. Maybe less. A pipe somewhere above it creaks like a ship.
It's FINE. It's so fine up here. You can see everything. You can see the whole thing. It's so beautiful it's stupid.

choices.label: Climb up and walk her back yourself

reaction.text: He climbs. The ladder is cold and gritty. Forty feet is very far when you're doing it in socks.
The catwalk moves under two people. He doesn't grab her; grabbing is how people fall. He sits down on the steel instead, right there, legs dangling over forty feet of nothing.
Sit with me. I'm scared. I'm actually really scared.
Don't touch me, Columbo.
I'm not touching you. I'm sitting. Sitting's legal.

It's true, and she hears that it's true, and she sits. And then he walks her in on her knees, one grid square at a time, talking the whole way about nothing, about Gerald, about Kevin, about how her sneakers on the stage look like two dropped commas, until her hand is on the ladder.
On the ladder down, one rung above him, she whispers it into his hair: "You came this time."
On the ladder down, one rung above him, she whispers it into his hair: "You came again."

choices.label: Film her back: “For my archive.”

reaction.text: He lifts his phone vertically, the way she does, the way she always does, and points it up at her.
For my archive!

Her own line, back at her, in her own voice. She laughs so hard she has to grab the rope with both hands, which is the point, and it's the laugh that brings her down: giddy, slow, rung by rung, by herself, still laughing.
On the stage she grabs his phone out of his hand to see the video. She watches herself, forty feet up, arms out, in the dark, lit by her own phone. She goes very quiet.
I look so happy.
She says it like it's evidence of a crime. Then she hands the phone back and puts her sneakers on, very carefully, and doesn't say anything else for a while.

choices.label: Shout from the stage: “I'm calling your mother.”

reaction.text: He holds up his phone, lit, Dr. Raman's contact on the screen, and shouts it up into the flies like a line from a play.
I'm calling your mother. Right now. I'm hitting the button, Raman.
Priya stops dead in the middle of the catwalk.
You already did that once this week!
Then she climbs down, fast and furious, nothing like careful, and comes across the stage barefoot and shoves him in the chest with both hands.
You WOULDN'T.
Try me.

She's shaking. Her whole body. She's also on the ground. Dev, in the front row, lets go of the seat, and exhales, the first breath he's taken in a minute, and sits down hard, and puts his face in his hands.

blocks.text: INT./EXT. FENNIMORE LIBRARY BELL TOWER. NIGHT (THU 11:50 P.M.)

Up a spiral staircase, two hundred and twelve steps, past a door that Yusuf opens with a look, to the bell chamber at the top of Fennimore's tower: the great bronze bells hanging in the dark like sleeping animals, pigeons shifting in the rafters, the wind coming through the louvers in slats.

And below, the whole town, lit. Mill Street's neon, red and blue. The white steeples. The Quad, silver. The Commons floodlit on its hill with WHITAKER across its face. And past all of it, the lake, black, a blade laid down in the dark.

The others stay a landing below. Dev and Yusuf are arguing, with great seriousness, about whether pigeons have feelings ("They mate for life, Yusuf." "So do barnacles."). Priya is asleep on the stairs, curled on her side, her head on Yusuf's folded gray hoodie, Kevin's beret over her face.
Simon and Cal at the louvers, side by side, elbows on the stone.

Simon asks about Richard. He doesn't say it like a question. He says it like a man reaching for something on a high shelf. What's he like. How does he laugh. Does he laugh. What does he order at a restaurant. Was he ever kind, even once, even by accident. He asks with a hunger Cal can feel coming off him like heat, and can't explain.
Why do you want to know?
I collect fathers. Other people's. Mine's a rumor.
He says it lightly. It doesn't come out light.

Cal knows Simon has a photograph of his father in a folder under a book of Plath. He watches Simon want his father, here, in the dark, a hundred feet up. He says nothing. He doesn't know what he'd say. He doesn't know what it means.
And don't read me up here. I'll jump, and it'll be your fault, and Priya will make a TikTok of it, and it'll do numbers.
Cal's phone buzzes in his pocket. 11:52.

Simon is watching his face. Simon is watching the phone. Simon can see the word Dad at the top of the screen, and he looks at it the way people look at a lit window from the street.

Commons sushi. Very convincing. I'd have believed you if I were a golden retriever.

He's good. God, he's good.
It's admiration. It's horror. Cal can't tell which, and he suspects neither can Simon.

He holds it out. Simon takes it like it's hot, both hands. The screen lights his face from below. For a second his thumbs hover over the keyboard. For a second he almost types. Cal sees his mouth move, like rehearsing the first word.
Then he gives it back. He's white.
God, no. No. I'd only tell him you have his jaw.

His hands are shaking. He puts them in his coat pockets. Cal leaves his father on read. Read 11:54 PM. The dots come and go three times, like someone knocking and then thinking better of it, and then they stop for good.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD-FLOOR HALLWAY. NIGHT (FRI 08-28, 1:07 A.M.)

Cal comes up the stairs of Lowell in his father's trousers and his own wet boxers, the navy jacket over his arm, shivering so hard his teeth click. Lake in his hair. Lake in his ears. He walked back across campus dripping, past the floodlit Commons, and a campus cop on a golf cart looked at him and decided not to know.

Cal comes up the stairs of Lowell in his father's suit, jacket over his arm, smelling of Stoli and cigar curtains and the lake, which he didn't touch, and which got on him anyway, the cold of it, the smell.

Cal comes up the stairs of Lowell in his father's suit, jacket over his arm, smelling of Stoli and cigar curtains. He keeps seeing a hand go white on a flashlight. He keeps seeing the beam drop onto the water and stay there.

Cal comes up the stairs of Lowell in Dev's Astros hoodie with tunnel grime on both knees and brick dust in his hair and a pigeon feather stuck to his shoulder that nobody told him about. He's still a little high on the bell tower, on the whole lit town. Priya bolted ahead of everyone on the walk back, half-running, saying she had to pee, saying she'd see them upstairs.
The hallway is dark except for the exit sign. Every door is shut.

And as he comes up the last flight, he hears it, through the bathroom door at the end of the hall. Under the sound of the tap running full. Someone being sick. Not drunk-sick, loud and comic and over. Careful. Practiced. Quiet, like it's done in a library.
His phone lights in his hand.

At the same moment the bathroom door opens and Priya comes out. Oversized T-shirt. Sleeves pulled down over her hands. Eyes red and wet. Behind her the tap is still running; she didn't turn it off. She's chewing mint gum, hard, fast, and the whole hallway smells like spearmint.
She sees him. She knows he heard. He knows she knows. It all happens in the time it takes the bathroom door to swing shut on its spring.
Commons sushi. Never again. I'm suing.

Commons sushi. The same lie he told his father an hour ago from a bell tower, word for word, in her mouth, for the same reason: so nobody has to deal with it. It lands in his stomach like a stone in a pond.

He knows her mother asked if she's eating. He knows the granola bar on her desk, and the wrap that doesn't exist, and her hands shaking on his phone. The sound through the door lands like a confirmation of something he already had and didn't want.
Then, smaller, standing in the hallway in her socks, picking at her sleeve:
I know you think I'm a monster. Stay up with me anyway? Gerald's being weird.
Stay up with me? Gerald's being weird.
Stay up with me? Gerald's being weird.
Gerald bangs, on cue, through the wall, like a man coughing in church.

And it's Monday again. He feels it in the floor. Bare feet at the end of a dock. jk. unless. His phone going into his pocket before he could see whether she answered. The same night, three days later, with the stakes face-up on the table.

He went to her last time. Into black water, in the dark, with his phone flashlight in his teeth. And now there's Margaux, the new thing, the bright thing, fifteen minutes away. The same choice, three days later, wearing a different coat.
Margaux's text sits on his screen. Fifteen minutes. Priya stands in the hallway with her sleeves over her hands and the tap still running behind her.

He walks to the stairs in the dark. She watches him go all the way down the first flight, until the turn of the banister takes him.

blocks.text: INT. KAPPA LAMBDA HOUSE, MARGAUX'S ROOM. NIGHT (FRI 1:25 A.M.)

The back door of the Kappa house is propped with a paperback copy of The Fountainhead, which feels like a joke someone is making at someone else's expense. Up the service stairs in the dark, a hallway of closed doors, a portrait of a disappointed woman from 1958. Her room, two doors down from the dormer. Hospital corners. Drawing tubes in the closet, door ajar.

Margaux is in his parka over a black slip, barefoot, sitting on the edge of the bed with her arms around her knees. Her face has been crying, or it's been about to. She isn't going to say which. The perfect girl is somewhere else tonight, on a hanger.
He hands her the sweatshirt. She drops it on the floor without looking at it, like the sweatshirt was never really the point.
You smell like the Rho. You went to Brooks's dinner. Of course you did. Everyone does.
And your hair's wet. Tell me he didn't take you to that dock. He did. Of course he did.
You skipped Brooks's dinner. I heard by ten-fifteen. He'll be unbearable for a week. Good.
Does your Priya know where you are right now?
Yes.
Then everybody will.

On the desk, under the lamp, a drawing she hasn't put away. Whitaker Commons, his grandfather's building, redone in glass: the fake buttresses gone, the walls gone, a roof floating on thin columns over a hall full of light. She sees him see it. She doesn't cover it. She lets him look. That's new. That's enormous.

She's lighter tonight, somehow. Something has come off her since the back stairs, a weight he can see the absence of. He thinks it's him. He doesn't know it's a text from her mother that said good girl.
She doesn't ask about his father. Not once. No Convocation, no trustees, no Nantucket. She asks something else, quietly, looking at her own bare feet.
Who'd you call? In the diary. The ice machine. Who'd you call?
It's the first question she's ever asked him that isn't on a list. He can tell. It comes from a different part of her, the way her real laugh did on Monday over the price tag.
He doesn't answer yet. She talks instead, for once, the way people talk at two in the morning, to fill the space where an answer should be. About Brooks.

People say Brooks and me like it's a sentence. Brooks-and-Margaux. It's not a sentence. It's a merger that never closed. Our mothers have been drafting it since we were in strollers. He's the only person who's ever looked at me the way you'd look at a house you were going to buy.
Her phone is face-down on the nightstand. It stays that way. Whatever's on it, she's letting it ring.

choices.label: Stay. Take your time with her.

reaction.text: He doesn't answer the question. He sits beside her on the bed and takes her face in his hands, slowly, like asking, and she lets him, and that's the answer to something.

It's not like Monday. Monday was a competition, both of them good at it and wanting the other to know. Tonight is slower. Her parka comes off his shoulders, then hers; the slip goes over her head with his hands, carefully, like taking something down from a high shelf. She's cold everywhere and then she isn't. She pulls him down on top of her and watches his face the whole time, eyes open, which she didn't do before, and when he moves inside her she says his name, just Cal, not Whitaker, not a joke, and holds on to the back of his neck like she's afraid of falling off the bed.

It's less like sex than a long, frank conversation between two people bad at conversations. She tells him what she wants without directions this time. He listens. At the end she bites his shoulder to keep from being loud, and then laughs into it, helplessly, the real laugh, the one she never uses.

After, she says into his shoulder that she never falls asleep first, never, it's a rule. Then she does, in the crook of his arm, in the middle of a sentence about the chapel. He lies awake and doesn't move his arm, even when it goes numb.
At 5:50 she wakes him with a hand on his chest. "You have to go before the house wakes up. Nobody knows." He goes, in the dark, with her smell on his hands.

choices.label: “Walk to breakfast with me tomorrow. In daylight.”

reaction.text: Walk to breakfast with me tomorrow. In daylight. Past Lorraine. Past your whole table. Just walk.
She looks at him like he's asked for a kidney. Like he's asked for one of hers, specifically, to keep in a jar.
No.
A long silence. He doesn't fill it. She looks at the phone face-down on the nightstand, and back at him, and at the drawing tubes in the closet.
Not yet.

It's the most hopeful thing she's ever said to him, and it's still no. He takes it. He stays. They don't sleep together; they lie on top of the hospital corners in their clothes and talk until four, about boarding schools, about nannies, about the 1791 chapel and why the proportions are wrong, and she draws it for him on the back of a Kappa formal invitation with an eyeliner pencil, in the dark, by phone light, and it's beautiful, and she tells him to throw it away, and he puts it in his pocket.

choices.label: Answer her: “I called my father. I was eleven.”

reaction.text: I called my father. I was eleven.
That's all. He doesn't say anything about his mother, or Maine, or the kite, or two weeks later. He just answers the question she asked, the way she asked it, and stops.

She doesn't comfort him. She doesn't say I'm sorry, or that must have been hard, or any of the sentences people keep in a drawer for this. She looks at the phone face-down on her nightstand for a long time.
Mine would have let it ring.
It's somehow the exact right answer. He doesn't know why. It goes into him like a key into a lock it was cut for.

They lie down side by side on top of the hospital corners in the dark, in their clothes, not touching, looking at the ceiling. At some point, he doesn't know when, she takes his hand. Neither of them mentions it. Neither of them will mention it at breakfast, where they won't sit together.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD-FLOOR HALLWAY. NIGHT (FRI 1:25 A.M.)

They sit on the hall carpet with their backs to the wall, the exit sign making everything red. Priya has her sleeves pulled down over her hands and her knees pulled up inside her T-shirt, like a tent. Mint gum. Chewing it slower now.
I didn't post it.
She says it to her knees. Not loud. Not angry anymore. Just put down on the carpet between them, like a thing she needs him to pick up or leave there.
She doesn't joke for a full minute. He counts. It's the longest she's ever gone. Gerald bangs, and she doesn't name it, doesn't give it a voice, doesn't do a bit. That's how he knows.
You came this time. Twice in one night. Don't make it a habit. I'll get used to it.
Then the dock. Finally. The true version, said lightly, which is how she says everything, which is how he knows it's the worst thing.

That night. The dock. I went under. On purpose. Just for like four seconds. To see. To see what it was like, if it was quiet. And then I came up. But I came up because it was cold. Not because I wanted to. That's the part I keep thinking about. That it was the cold that did it. Not me.

That night. When you pulled me out. Everybody thinks I slipped. I didn't slip. I went under. On purpose. Just for like four seconds. To see. And I would've come up anyway, I think, because it was so cold. Not because I wanted to. That's the part I keep thinking about.
The tap's off now. The hallway is so quiet he can hear the exit sign hum.
She turns her head on the wall and looks at him. Her face is very young without the performance on it, like a stage with the set struck.
Tell me something true back. Please. I'm not going to make it if you're charming right now. If you do a bit I'll scream.

blocks.text: INT. BROOKS HADLEY'S ROOM, RHO HOUSE, TOP FLOOR. NIGHT (FRI 2:30 A.M.)

Every light is on. The overhead. The desk lamp. Both bedside lamps. A phone flashlight lying face-up on the nightstand, pointed at the ceiling like a little searchlight. The room is bright as an operating theater, at two-thirty in the morning, on the top floor of the oldest house on Elm Row.

Brooks sits on the edge of his bed in his dinner shirt, collar open, shoes still on. One hand flat on his sternum. He's breathing in a pattern, deliberate, counted: four in. Hold. Eight out. Four in. Hold. Eight out. His lips move on the numbers. His eyes are fixed on a spot on the floor that has nothing on it.
It takes a long time. Then it passes, the way weather passes, and his shoulders come down.
He takes out his phone and opens a thread. The contact is saved as two initials: R.W.
